title: Recon / Service Enumeration
source: Project-authored (obol-local). Common-knowledge service-enumeration methodology; independent expression, not derived from any third-party card set. References cite public tool docs / HackTricks.

actions.title: Anonymous SMB Enumeration
actions.hypothesis: 445/139 is worth probing before anything else: many hosts still allow a null or guest session, which hands you the share list, a RID-cycled account list, and occasionally readable files — all without a credential. Cheap, quiet, and often the first real lead.
actions.proves: the anonymous SMB surface — shares reachable without auth and/or a RID-cycled user list
actions.does_not_prove: authenticated SMB access, a working credential, or a shell — a null session is disclosure, not access

commands.note: List shares over a null session; if the empty user is rejected, retry as guest with an empty password.
Same idea with read/write flags shown, so a writable share stands out immediately.
Cycle RIDs through the guest session to recover the full account list with no Kerberos traffic.
One-shot sweep of shares, users, groups, and password policy over RPC.

actions.title: Web Service Triage
actions.hypothesis: Fingerprint the stack before you fuzz it. The server, framework, and any CMS decide which wordlist and which checks are worth running; guessing blind wastes the noisy budget you'd rather spend once you know what you're looking at.
actions.proves: the web stack fingerprint — server software, framework, and CMS/tech markers
actions.does_not_prove: any vulnerability, hidden path, or access — a fingerprint only points you at the right next check

commands.note: Aggressive fingerprint; switch the scheme to https for 443.
Raw response headers — server banner, powered-by, redirects, and cookies at a glance.

actions.title: DNS Enumeration & Zone Transfer
actions.hypothesis: A nameserver that answers a zone transfer (AXFR) simply gives you the internal host map. Even when AXFR is refused, record enumeration still surfaces mail hosts, subdomains, and the shape of the domain.
actions.proves: DNS records, and — where the server is misconfigured — a full zone transfer (the internal host map)
actions.does_not_prove: access of any kind; DNS data is reconnaissance

commands.note: The transfer attempt; a full record dump means AXFR is open and should be reported.
Standard record enumeration plus the AXFR attempt in a single run.

actions.title: SNMP Enumeration
actions.hypothesis: UDP/161 is slow to scan and routinely skipped, so it's a favourite hiding spot for useful data. Find a readable community string ('public' is the usual first guess) and the MIB leaks processes, accounts, routes, and sometimes credentials embedded in config values.
actions.proves: a readable SNMP community string and the system information it exposes
actions.does_not_prove: device control or a validated OS credential — SNMP read access is information disclosure

commands.note: Spray community strings first — you need a valid one before walking anything.
Walk the tree with the community you found (defaults to 'public').
A tidier, sectioned view — accounts, processes, network, installed software.

actions.title: IKE / IPSec VPN Enumeration
actions.hypothesis: An IKE endpoint that still accepts aggressive mode returns a PSK hash inside the handshake, which you can crack offline. UDP/500 is easy to overlook on a scan; when it's open, that PSK is often the entire objective.
actions.proves: an aggressive-mode IKE handshake that yields a crackable PSK hash
actions.does_not_prove: the PSK plaintext or any VPN access — the hash must be cracked, then the credential validated

report.finding: IPSec VPN Endpoint with Aggressive Mode

commands.note: Fingerprint the endpoint in main mode first.
Aggressive mode; writes the captured PSK hash to ike-psk.txt when the endpoint permits it.
Dictionary-crack the captured hash offline.

actions.title: Finger Service User Enumeration
actions.hypothesis: The finger service (TCP/79) will tell you which accounts exist. It's uncommon, but on older Unix targets it's a free, unauthenticated way to build a username list for spraying.
actions.proves: system usernames disclosed by the finger service
actions.does_not_prove: a credential or access — a username is spray material, not a login

commands.note: Show currently logged-in users.
Probe a named account to confirm it exists and read its shell/home.

actions.title: VNC Enumeration
actions.hypothesis: An exposed VNC service (5900/5901) is worth checking for no-auth access or a known auth bypass. Read the authentication mode first — a passwordless VNC is a straight desktop, but you confirm that by connecting, not by assuming.
actions.proves: VNC exposure and its authentication mode
actions.does_not_prove: desktop access — a no-auth or bypassed VNC has to be connected to and confirmed by hand before any access is claimed

commands.note: Report the auth mode and check the RealVNC bypass; a hit is a lead to verify, not proof.
Connect manually — this is where access is actually confirmed, by hand.

actions.title: SMTP User Enumeration
actions.hypothesis: A mail server that honours VRFY/EXPN/RCPT will confirm which usernames are real — a quiet oracle that feeds a spray list. An open relay, if present, is a separate finding worth its own note.
actions.proves: valid mailbox/user names disclosed via VRFY/RCPT
actions.does_not_prove: a credential, relay abuse, or access — the names are spray material only

commands.note: Probe with VRFY; fall back to -M RCPT when VRFY is disabled.
Drive a manual transaction, which also reveals relay behaviour.

actions.title: FTP Enumeration
actions.hypothesis: Anonymous FTP or a world-readable/writable directory is a classic entry point: configs, backups, and source drop straight into your loot, and a writable directory that maps to a webroot can stage a shell.
actions.proves: the FTP access surface — anonymous login and any readable files
actions.does_not_prove: a working credential, write access, or a foothold — a directory listing is loot, not a shell

commands.note: Check anonymous login across the host.
List the root directory over anonymous FTP.
Interactive session: log in anonymous/anonymous, then ls, get, and test put for a writable directory.

actions.title: POP3 / IMAP Enumeration
actions.hypothesis: A mail service (POP3 110/995, IMAP 143/993) discloses its software and capabilities, and the NTLM-info NSE scripts leak the AD domain and host name the same way SMB does. Mail is also where credentials and password-reset material live, so a validated login is high value — read the capabilities first, then log in with any credential you already hold.
actions.proves: the mail service's version + capabilities, and any NTLM-disclosed domain/host
actions.does_not_prove: a credential or mailbox access — capabilities are recon; reading mail needs a validated login (which the credential lane provides)

commands.note: Capabilities + version; the *-ntlm-info scripts disclose the domain/host name on an AD-joined mail server (spray/context material).
Read the IMAPS banner/cert directly (use :995 for POP3S). The cert CN/SAN often names the real host.
With a held credential, list the mailbox (imaps for IMAP, pop3s://…/1 for POP3). Mail is a classic place to find further creds/reset links.

actions.title: RDP Enumeration (nxc)
actions.hypothesis: RDP (3389) discloses the host/domain name and its NLA/auth mode unauthenticated, and — with a credential or NT hash you already hold — netexec validates access over RDP and grabs a login screenshot. A `[+]` (or `pwned!`) is confirmed access material; open the session to use it. Pass-the-hash works against RDP when Restricted Admin is enabled.
actions.proves: RDP exposure, its NLA/auth mode, and — with a credential — validated access + a screenshot
actions.does_not_prove: an interactive desktop — a netexec `[+]` is validated login material; the RDP session (sessions layer) is where access is actually taken and proven

commands.note: Unauthenticated: netexec prints the host name, domain, OS build and NLA state — context with zero credentials and no lockout risk.
Validate a held credential over RDP. Mind account lockout — this is a login attempt, so approve it deliberately.
Pass-the-hash over RDP (works when Restricted Admin mode is enabled) — no plaintext needed.
Grab a login/desktop screenshot as a lead/proof (a logged-in session sometimes screenshots straight to the desktop).
Open the interactive session — this is where desktop access is actually taken (use /pth:{{nthash}} instead of /p for pass-the-hash).

actions.title: NFS Share Enumeration (nxc)
actions.hypothesis: An NFS server (2049) exports directories that are frequently world-readable or mountable with a forged UID. List the exports, mount them, and read — and note any export without root_squash, which is a direct privesc lead (mount, drop a SUID root binary, run it).
actions.proves: the exported NFS shares and their access options (e.g. no_root_squash)
actions.does_not_prove: file access or privesc — mount and read to confirm; a no_root_squash export is a lead the privesc lane turns into root, not proof on its own

commands.note: netexec lists the exports and their permissions in one shot; add --enum-shares for a recursive listing of readable files.
The classic export list. Watch for `*` (world) or a broad CIDR, and for missing root_squash.
Mount an export read it. On a no_root_squash export you can plant a SUID-root binary from your box and execute it on the target for root.
